But because of our loss-aversion, we seek certainty. We want to be as safe as possible with our bets. This goes for our money, and it goes for everything else that we do.

Full certainty puts those decisions into a different category. The things that we can be fully certain about. As developers, these things are few and far between. It's not bad news. And that's what we're talking about today. How to embrace this uncertainty.

Very often we try to sell certainty. This is such a common business practice. We want to sell a given product with all the features that you want for a fixed price and within a fixed timeline. All of these things mitigating uncertainty.

and ultimately viewing uncertainty as the enemy. But perhaps there's another way to do this. Perhaps we can embrace uncertainty. And instead of selling certainty, we sell change. Change is progressive.

Change is adaptive. If we sell change as a valuable aspect of what we do, we get a chance to create a scenario where adapting to a new market is easy, where adapting to a new staffing situation becomes second nature.

Thanks to this unified approach, we get full visibility into every step of the critical user path, exactly as it behaves in the production version. After the nightly run finishes, an N8N workflow starts at 10am and analyzes all collected startup metrics.

If any value exceeds our threshold, currently set to 4.5 seconds, the system immediately sends an alert to Slack. The biggest advantage is timing. We now discover regressions directly in, before release branching even starts. That gives engineers enough time to investigate and fix problems before regression testing begins.

We also maintain dashboards for long-term trend analysis and visual monitoring. An interesting side effect appeared when we migrated to Xcode 26. Startup times on simulators suddenly increased overnight. At first, we suspected a regression in our codebase. Later, we discovered that simulators in Xcode 26 had becomes lower overall.

The slowdown affected every stage of the startup flow, while real devices remained unchanged. Without historical performance tracking, identifying this would have been much harder. Why we intentionally slowed down the internet in C. It seemed like the problem was solved, performance tests were running every night, alerts were coming into Slack, and we could track trends in a dashboard. But at some point after another release, we again saw a regression in app launch time for users.

A natural question came up, why did the issue still reach production if we already had automated performance tests in place? This time, startup degradation only affected users with slow internet connections. The application relies heavily on request caching to reduce the time between launch and reaching the target screen. In one release, the cache mechanism broke silently, forcing the application to wait for fresh server responses before entering the UI.

On fast office Wi-Fi, the issue was almost invisible. For users with unstable or slow connections, startup time increased dramatically. After that incident, we redesigned the test execution flow. The new process works like this. 1. The first 10 runs execute under normal network conditions. 2. During these runs, the application fills local caches. 3. Then the network is artificially degraded, bandwidth limited to 400 kilobits per second.

Latency increased to 200 miz. 4. The same scenarios execute again with cached data already present on the device. To emulate poor network conditions, we use Network Link Conditioner. This tool throttles the entire device network stack instead of individual requests, which makes the environment much closer to real-world usage.

This approach gives us two important validations simultaneously. First, if a new unexpected network request appears in the critical path, startup time immediately increases. Second, we automatically verify cache correctness. If caching works properly, startup performance remains nearly identical even under slow network conditions. If the app suddenly waits for the backend again, the regression becomes obvious.

Recently, this setup caught a subtle but critical issue. One developer modified logic inside the caching layer. During code review, the mistake looked almost harmless. From the code itself, it was difficult to predict any major impact.

예를 들어 IT업계에서 개발자가 프로젝트 매니저가 되거나 또 병원에서 임상업무 대신 행정업무를 맡는 방식인데요. 기존 산업에 대한 이해가 있기 때문에 새로운 일을 배우는 부담이 상대적으로 적다는 장점이 있습니다.
이어서 세 번째, 같은 직무를 유지하면서 업계만 바꾸는 겁니다. 회계사가 제조업에서 의료분야로 옮기거나 마케팅 담당자가 금융회사에서 교육기관으로 이직하는 것처럼 기존의 경험을 살리면서 새로운 환경을 경험하는 방법입니다. 업무는 익숙하지만 새로운 환경과 문화를 경험할 수 있어서 가장 현실적인 이직 방법 가운데 하나로 손꼽힙니다.
SICK은 이 세 가지 가운데 어느 것이 가장 좋은 방법이라고 말하지는 않고 있습니다. 대신 중요한 것은 자신의 상황과 목표에 맞는 선택을 하는 것이라고 강조합니다. 또한 이직을 꼭 처음부터 다시 시작하는 것으로 생각할 필요도 없다고 조언합니다. 지금까지 쌓아온 경험과 기술은 생각보다 훨씬 다양한 분야에서 활용될 수 있기 때문입니다.
결국 성공적인 이직은 단순히 회사를 옮기는 것이 아니라 자신의 강점과 가치관을 이해하고 또 그것을 가장 잘 살릴 수 있는 새로운 환경을 찾는 과정입니다. 지금 새로운 출발을 고민하고 있다면 먼저 어디로 갈까 보다 나는 어떤 사람인가를 스스로 물어보는 것이 성공적인 커리어 전환의 첫걸음이 될 수 있습니다.
더 많은 이야기가 궁금하신가요? 애플 포드캐스트, 구글 포드캐스트, 스포티파이 또는 여러분의 포드캐스트를 통해 만나보세요.

They come here in desperate search of something they need, something that's almost impossible to find where they live. They're looking for a dentist, one that they can afford.

Every day, thousands of people, mostly American, mostly white, and mostly retired, come to this town looking for relief from the turmoil in their mouths. Here, dental care costs up to 80% less than what it might cost in the US. Dental tourism to Los Algodones is so common that many call this place Molar City. Today, there are nearly 1,000 dentists in this 7,000-person town, and 98% of those in the patient's chair traveled here from outside Mexico. Lasha is going to take it from here.

Watch any one of these YouTube videos, and you'll see how a trip to Molar City is made easy for an American. For decades, this crossing didn't even require a passport. In one video, a retired couple arrives at Arizona's edge. They do a 360, displaying the massive lot where they've just parked. "We love Mexico," they say emphatically, talking to the camera. The camera then pans to show the rust-colored border wall in front of them. That corrugated monstrosity. They marvel. Then a US Border Patrol vehicle starts driving past the screen, on guard, it seems, for anyone trying to cross in the opposite direction. To this, the camera woman speaks again, as if she's talking directly to Border Patrol. "Get 'em, boys," she says. Then they begin their walk into Mexico. In Los Algodones, there are dense clusters of medical offices and a canopy of billboards above them. Vendors are set up on sidewalks where they sell handmade goods and kitschy souvenirs, like this one graphic tee that says, "Keep calm, you're on the fun side of Trump's wall." And then there are the street promoters, people who are stationed at almost every street corner. Each of them competing for superlatives: the best deal, the quickest appointment, the most popular clinic in town. In Molar City, a street promoter is the first person a tourist will encounter.

If a given restaurant has the capacity to, let's say, seat 150 people, but their processes, the way that they route their servers, for example, don't allow for that number of people to be served,

we have a mismatch in the capacity and the ability. On the other hand, you can also have the opposite problem, where you have a highly efficient waitstaff and simply not enough room to maximize that ability. In this case, your ability outpaces your capacity.

Keen listeners will recognize that this episode is coming out on a Tuesday, whereas usually episodes of the show come out on Mondays and Wednesdays and Fridays. And in fact, we've missed our Friday refills for two weeks in a row. This is a capacity problem.

Certainly with over 900 episodes of the show published, I have very likely have the ability to execute on these episodes. But because my time has been constrained, for example, yesterday, my son ended up having a fever. And so I had to spend my time doing family things rather than recording for the podcast. My capacity was limited. So why is this important?

As you go through your career, you're going to have numerous occasions where these two things will be aligned. But then you're going to have a lot of occasions where they're not aligned. And here's the critical thing. You may not actually know. You may not know that your capacity is the limiting factor or that your ability is the limiting factor.

By having this lens available, you can ask the question, is my capacity the limiting factor in this scenario? You can ask this for teams as well. The most simple example, of course, is having a highly efficient team but not having enough people on the team.

It's important to understand also that as you change one factor, another factor may change. And that your capacity is not something that you can't change. We aren't talking about external factors that are out of your control. Instead, we're talking about longer-term setup factors.

Another simple example of this is that perhaps you have the capacity to work in a particular language. You've proven this by working in that language in the past. But since it's been a while since you worked in that language, it's possible that if it came down to it in the moment, you wouldn't have the ability. And some of this is just because

Our abilities change over time. We lose abilities. They may decay with a lack of use. And the same is true if you were to imagine that you have the capacity to work in a language that you've never worked in before. In other words, if you were to learn that language, you could develop the ability to work in that language.

Another way to think about capacity is to imagine that it's similar to potential. And on the flip side, you can imagine that ability is similar to performance. You have performance and you have potential. And it should be noted that these things can change even on a day-to-day basis. systems affect everything in the system. There's very few decisions that won't affect something else, both adversely and positively. This is true for even the smallest of actions.

Even the smallest thing like an emoji. This seems crazy, but the emojis that you send to people's Slack messages, or if you send GIFs back in text message threads, these are reinforcement mechanisms. These are ways of expressing yourself, and the other person will receive these expressions as feedback on their actions.
You can either positively reinforce actions that have positive effects on your team, or you can positively reinforce actions that have negative effects on your team.

And then you can also use the other side, negative reinforcement on things that may have negative impact on your team. And as it turns out, even though it's not intuitive, we often provide negative reinforcement for behaviors that could have positive impacts on our team. This is the example that we talked about earlier where we encourage someone to withdraw, to not bring their ideas to the table by shooting them down too harshly.
So it's important to kind of create some heuristics for yourself. For example, it's very likely that a good heuristic is to avoid negative feedback unless something is relatively critical.

Negative feedback is a very strong mechanism that we can use in the workplace. The reason for that is because given enough negative feedback, a person may fear that their job is in danger. This is especially true for managers.

And so negative feedback ends up speaking much louder than positive feedback. Positive feedback may give me the hope of some kind of better position, maybe a raise. But the downside of getting fired is much larger than the upside of getting a raise.

Motiviert durch Aufregung und Adrenalin.

Aseguran que estos ataques, bajo el pretexto de que las lanchas transportan drogas, constituyen una violación de los derechos humanos. Como nos cuenta Ana María Islas, estos hechos siguen sin una respuesta oficial por parte de Estados Unidos.

Está quemada la embarcación. El 17 de marzo, la embarcación ecuatoriana Negra Francisca Duarte II, con 16 pescadores a bordo, fue atacada con drones a 170 millas náuticas de las Islas Galápagos, en el Pacífico Oriental, mientras regresaba de semanas de pesca.

Los sobrevivientes señalan como responsables a fuerzas militares estadounidenses. Nos atacaron los americanos. Nosotros ya veníamos de regreso a tierra. Y los drones andaban arriba, que nos daban vuelta. Está quemada la embarcación. La embarcación fue hundida y los pescadores, encapuchados y esposados en una patrulla marítima. Nos dijeron, si levanten las manos, nos apuntaron.

Tras ser retenidos y trasladados por horas, fueron entregados a autoridades salvadoreñas en calidad de náufragos. Es el peor error de ellos, habernos atacado a nosotros sin tener nada. Los 16 fueron repatriados sin cargos penales a Ecuador, pero no fueron los únicos.

Nueve días después, otro barco ecuatoriano, el Don Maca, con 20 pescadores a bordo, fue alcanzado por un dron a 750 millas náuticas al norte del puerto de Manta, Ecuador. Un ataque similar al de la Negra Francisca. Porque veíamos que la patrulla se venía acercando. El dron y un dron más grande estaba alrededor que los daba vuelta.

Los sobrevivientes refieren haber identificado tanto en la patrulla como en los uniformes de los militares e insignias de Estados Unidos, además de que hablaban en inglés y viajaban con traductores. Ambos casos podrían dar pistas de lo que ocurrió con el barco pesquero Fiorella, que desapareció con ocho de sus tripulantes el 20 de enero.

Ninguno de estos tres hechos aparece en el registro público de la Operación Lanza del Sur, que encabeza el Departamento de Guerra en el Caribe y Pacífico Oriental. Hasta el momento, el Pentágono no ha provisto a NMAS Univisión la información solicitada sobre este caso. Mientras no tengas nada, no pasa nada.

Los pescadores han documentado inspecciones estadounidenses en aguas ecuatorianas como esta, al barco Volga II. Tras 14 horas, la tripulación fue liberada sin cargos. En tanto nadie se hace responsable de estos hechos, estos relatos elevan cuestionamientos sobre la posible participación de Estados Unidos en detenciones arbitrarias y uso extrajudicial de la fuerza, impactando a comunidades pesqueras de la región.

This simple idea was introduced to me by a friend of mine here in Chattanooga. His name is Chris Keithley. We were hanging out at a rupee meetup here in Chattanooga that I organized. And Chris introduced me to this idea, and I think it's really useful. I think it's going to be valuable to you. First, I want to talk a little bit about some of the problems that this idea is going to solve.

Have you ever spent time in your code trying to figure out, trying to walk through each step and figure out what exactly is happening at a given step? Sure, this is applicable in many different situations, but trying to keep information in your mind about exactly what things are happening at that given point in time can

That's a little bit hard to do because you are not the computer. In fact, you are simply writing the code that explains what you want the computer to do. Functional programming languages try to fix this problem by eliminating the idea of mutable state. The word mutable means that the state can change. Now imagine that you have, for example, a class level variable.

And that class level variable determines how a particular function runs. Maybe you have an if statement in that function that checks that class variable to determine what to do inside of that function.

Now, of course, I'm using the word function and method interchangeably here in this conversation, but the idea is very simple. It's that there is something outside of that method that determines what is going to happen on the inside of that method. And as you're writing that method, if you have things outside of that method that determine what will happen on the inside of that method, then when you're reading that...

you have to consider those things without actually seeing them. In other words, the state is difficult to determine, and the outcome of running a particular method becomes even more difficult to determine. This is perhaps one of the hardest parts of object-oriented design, and it's one of the things that you have to be aware of, and there are ways around this problem. There are ways to subvert the hard parts in this problem.

Have you ever found yourself writing a test that sets up a scenario? For example, creating a user and signing that user in and then visiting a page, maybe using something like Capybara if you're using Rails. And you sign that person in, you visit a page, you fill out a form, and then you do all of these things to set up the state just to check a single method.

Now let me be clear, sometimes integration tests exactly like this are important and you should be creating those for the most critical paths in your application. But if you have to write a test, if you have to set up state in order to check a method,

then there could be something wrong with the way your code is organized. In a minute, we're going to discuss two things that you can do to make your code a little bit easier to reason about and to get you away from relying on state, to get you away from holding everything in your head so that when you read your methods and when you are testing your methods, you don't rely so much on the external state and instead you rely on what exactly is happening in that method.

Margaret Atwood's sequel to The Handmaid's Tale, which is called The Testaments, had a worldwide release date of September 10th. And it was a strictly embargoed title. And what that means is everybody who wanted to sell the book had to sign an affidavit where they swore to not sell it or release it or even talk about having it before September 10th. We signed these documents a couple times a year for really big titles. It was the strictest of these I had ever seen.

We were supposed to keep the boxes of books in a locked and monitored location. We couldn't even post pictures of the boxes to social media. And the publisher, Penguin Random House, wanted this book to be a mystery until it arrived on September 10th, to be totally secret.

But then last week, about eight days before September 10th, people started posting pictures on social media that they had gotten their copies from Amazon. Copies they preordered on Amazon started arriving. It's unclear how many went out. But what happened was that that basically gave people permission to run their reviews.

And so as soon as that happened, the New York Times and NPR put reviews on their website. People who had exclusive excerpts ran them early. And so the kind of mystique around the book was punctured a little bit. Meanwhile, indie bookstores still had to wait. And there's this kind of worldwide impression that if you had ordered this from Amazon, you would have gotten it first while we're here trying to play by the rules and keep our boxes of books in a locked closet.
And so for sales, like what is the downside for you for sales? Is it like a reputation hit or is does it actually translate into something kind of more immediate?

One of the dangerous parts, as I mentioned, is the impression that Amazon can get it to you earlier. So I don't know how many people who are planning on buying it from a bookstore went to Amazon instead in hopes that they ordered it early. And I'm not sure there's a way we can find that out. But part of it is if they had successfully kept the mystery up, there would have been a lot of intrigue about that book and people would buy it just to find out what happened. I mean, that mystery can drive people into a bookstore to buy the book. Here's a couple of Danny's tweets from the Raven account about the Margaret Atwood desktop.

It should come as no surprise that a certain huge online retailer is selling this book very close to our cost. If we sold it at their price, we'd make $1.73 per copy. We've discussed before how this is unfair and how we deal with it. But now, not only is the huge online retailer selling it for a price we can't compete with, but they shipped out copies a week early. This increases the likelihood that someone who got it early uploads a bootleg copy online, cutting into sales for everyone.

We're doing fine on this particular title, in part because that Twitter thread led a bunch of people to pre-order it from us, which we love and appreciate. But if this was a regular thing, people would just start buying new release books only from Amazon. Or places like Walmart or Target would feel like they had permission to put it out early, too. And then we would really lose sales if this turned into a pattern.

And on the thread where you discuss this, you mentioned that the indie bookstore industry really relies on these fall and pre-holiday blockbusters to kind of get you through the year. Right. AI takes center stage at BioAsia 2026 in Hyderabad as Asia's leading life sciences and health tech forum opens its 23rd edition with a sharp focus on AI, automation, and data science to accelerate healthcare innovation. More than 175 exhibitors spanning pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medtech, digital health, and advanced manufacturing showcase a broad tech-bio ecosystem. The event brings researchers, entrepreneurs, investors, and policymakers together to push the tech-bio revolution and address global health challenges. Telangana highlights its strong policies, skilled workforce, and premier educational institutions as key drivers of growth in life sciences. The opening ceremony, led by the State Chief Minister, included the Genome Valley Excellence Award for Cancer Gene Therapy to Professor Bruce L. Levine. Inauguration and awards underscore Telangana's leadership in life sciences and recognize Levine's work in cancer gene therapy. Telangana also unveiled initiatives such as the Young India Skills University and the Telangana School of Life Sciences to build talent in mRNA technology, gene therapy, and AI. Recent moves cited include the Telangana Next Gen Life Sciences Policy, Genome Valley expansion, the launch of OneBio and multiple global capability centers in Hyderabad, The event emphasized ongoing collaborations among research institutions, corporates, startups, MSMEs, and government to create a trusted, future-ready life sciences ecosystem in Telangana. Telangana Rising 2047 envisions making the state a $1 trillion economy by year 2034 and $3 trillion by year 2047 through cross-sector collaboration across research labs, industry, startups, MSMEs, and government. The Telangana Life Sciences Policy 2026-30 promotes cross-border collaboration, international capital, and translation of breakthroughs into healthcare solutions to position Telangana as a global life sciences hub. Plans include shifting from supply-led manufacturing to solution-driven leadership by building talent in mRNA, gene editing, and AI-driven drug discovery, while boosting Hyderabad's role in medical tourism.

Unilever is partnering with a major cloud provider to run an AI-first digital overhaul, migrating its data and cloud platform to Google Cloud to speed demand generation and deliver actionable insights. The initiative centers on flagship brands Dove, Vaseline, and Hellmann's as consumer journeys become more AI-driven and conversational, aiming to redefine how consumer packaged goods are discovered and shopped. Leaders describe it as a milestone in modernizing legacy systems and boosting agility and consumer engagement in the CPG sector. Market reaction showed UL trading near its 52-week high, with a pre-market around $74.65 and approaching the annual high of $74.97. Unilever reported strong fiscal 2025 results, with total sales up 3.8% to €50.5 billion across Beauty Wellbeing, personal care, and home care. The collaboration is framed as part of a broader shift toward agentic consumer journeys where AI surfaces influence product discovery and selection. It aims to redefine how brands are found and purchased, aligning with increasingly conversational journeys guided by intelligent digital agents. There is mention of repurposing a former Unilever soap factory in Wales into a modular data center site, signaling broader data infrastructure development alongside the cloud migration. The initiative seeks more personalized consumer engagement and more efficient marketing investments, signaling a move toward AI-driven experiences in the CPG space. Unilever's longstanding relationship with Accenture, renewed in 2024 to scale GenAI, complements Horizon 3 Labs' efforts in Toronto that reportedly runs hundreds of AI applications. The partnership signals a broader industry shift toward AI-enabled transformation in marketing, data infrastructure, and automated business processes within consumer goods, with overhauls of marketing processes to establish new measurement standards, increase conversion rates, and accelerate AI adoption across global.

The ASM AI Fest 2026 runs through February 28th, showcasing an AI-first mindset across teaching, research, learning methods, and administration to prepare graduates and staff for pervasive AI adoption. The festival features world-class AI workshops that move beyond awareness to practical AI applications, aiming for AI to amplify human capability rather than substitute it. It concludes with a closing ceremony on February 28th, reinforcing ASM's leadership in AI-integrated education across MBA, PGDM, MCA, engineering, undergraduate studies, and school and junior college. A press release includes a photo and logo link and carries an advertorial disclaimer noting the content was provided by PR Newswire and not authored by Business Standard journalists. The initiative is described as one of the region's largest AI-driven academic efforts and positions ASM as a pioneer in AI-integrated education aligned with national AI objectives. As part of the sustained transformation, ASM will form institute-wide AI task forces, establish the ASM AI Center of Excellence, deploy the Navdrishti app for automated student lifecycle management, and introduce AI into PGDM dual specialization programs. The long-term roadmap includes institute-wise AI task forces, a center of excellence for training and research, and the Navdrishti app with AI-enabled placements and broader expansion into academics and finances. Institutional AI roadmap highlights creating task forces, a COE for training and research, and Navdrishti for automated student lifecycle management, with initial AI-enabled placements and later expansion. AI integration spans the entire ASM academic spectrum, from MBA, PGEM, MCA, and engineering to undergraduate and school junior college, preparing learners for a future with pervasive AI adoption. A PGDM dual specialization program with AI integration was launched, signaling program-level AI incorporation across curricula. Program implications include AI-driven analytics for MBA PGDM, ML tools for MCA engineering, AI-influenced entrepreneurship, and data-driven decisions for undergraduates, and foundational AI literacy for younger students. The initiative aligns with India's India AI Mission and Digital India, aiming to position India as a global hub for AI talent and to embed AI across education and administration.

Ant Group expands its open-source AI family with two trillion-parameter models, Ling-2.5-1T and Ring-2.5-1T, released under open licenses on Hugging Face and ModelScope. The move continues Ling's ecosystem expansion following Ling 2.0 unveiled in late 2025 and positions Ant Group as a key proponent of open AI distribution for researchers and developers. Ling-2.5-1T is described as a flagship general language model focused on efficient reasoning and agent interaction, capable of handling context lengths up to 1 million tokens while using about 5,890 tokens to reach frontier-like results. Ring-2.5-1T is a reasoning-optimized model with a hybrid linear architecture, delivering strong mathematical performance on IMO 2025 and CMO 2025 benchmarks. Both models are part of a coordinated Ling, Ring, and Ming strategy aimed at enterprise AI deployments that combine language understanding, reasoning, and multimodal capabilities for financial services. The open-release approach seeks to accelerate ecosystem adoption by enabling external developers to build domain-specific finance applications, potentially reducing costs and enabling larger-scale deployments. Ant Group frames these releases within a broader fintech trend of integrating large language models and reasoning systems into tasks such as compliance, customer interactions, and risk assessment. Open Access Positions: Ant Group among global contributors to open large-scale AI and supports adapting models for financial domain tasks by external developers. The Ling-2.5-1T release emphasizes efficient reasoning and agent interaction, while Ring-2.5-1T targets higher-order mathematical reasoning and benchmark performance. Overall, the announcements underscore a move toward open, collaborative AI infrastructure designed to support enterprise-grade finance use.

It positions AI-enabled capabilities as industry agnostic, bridging AI investments with real business outcomes through ongoing enterprise adoption and scale. Measured outcomes include roughly 12% improvement in associate retention, 6 to 8% reductions in average handle time, 100% compliance accuracy within 60 days, a 23% rise in Net Promoter Score, and a 10% lift in sales conversion rates. And then Windows has a similar sort of construct with its own run loop. And you've done something to make those work. So UIKit wants to be in control, and XAML also wants to be in control.

And what we've done is basically link them together. We've put XAML at the head of it. XAML gets events first. But since they're both event-based, whenever one of them drains their event queue, it yields to the other one. And whenever that one drains its event queue, it yields back to XAML. So whether you're touch events or whatever else, whether they're coming in from the UIKit side or the XAML side, they are all routed to the correct place.

And the reason that's actually super important is especially when you're talking about UI. You kind of want both UI worlds living in the same thread so that everything is in sync, all your animations, all your transitions. You wouldn't want all your XAML effects happening first, and then like 200 milliseconds later, all your core animation stuff happens. All of that has to be in lockstep and sync. And this was just a really great solution that some of our guys came with.

You also showed a UI where you can have UIKit stuff in a view hierarchy, so it's inside of a XAML object, and then that XAML object's inside of a UIKit object. So you can just mix and match them. It's not like a window that shows your UIKit stuff, and then they're not. So this is very much, we're not taking an iOS app and skinning it, and there's no emulation going on here. There's no middle layer that's doing anything.

It's really a native experience, and because of that, you have one compositor that's rendering all of the UI, whether that's coming from XAML or UIKit. You have one run loop, and events get to the right place no matter where they came in from.

What was once a town of about 750 when Magaña first arrived is now crammed with clinics, hotels, restaurants, and pharmacies. Today, young dentists and souvenir vendors from all over Mexico continue to migrate to town in hopes of finding stable work. And the tourists keep coming in droves.

In winter, it's too much people and they make lines, and that's uncomfortable for them, but they don't care. They make the lines, you know, and they still coming because they find dental services good, a good price and everything, and very handsome doctors. We live from the tourists, you know.

We live from the tourists. It's a sentiment I heard from everyone in town. Teenagers will run to the border after school to sell trinkets to people waiting in line to go home. Women will walk up and down the line selling handmade sweaters and hot meals. And on the American side, the Quechan Tribe manages a casino resort. It's a popular spot for dental tourists who try their hand at the slot machines in between appointments.

Street promoter Alberto moved back to the area 8 years ago, in part to be closer to his family after a road accident in Cancún made it difficult for him to walk. For molars, we vary anywhere from $120 to some of us— some of us are making like $500 or $800 a week.

I think dental has helped Algodones a lot, but I think people just make their money and they go somewhere else, you know? They go live it up somewhere else. Because a lot of these doctors have become millionaires.

Many of those original dentists live in mansions complete with indoor courtyards and pools. In addition to their dental practice, certain families in town own many of the hotels, restaurants, and pharmacies here. But zoom out of the town center and you'll see mostly unpaved roads and humble homes. There's this 18th-century paleontologist, Georges Cuvier. He has this famous quote about teeth. "Show me your teeth," he said, "and I will tell you who you are." It's true. That from teeth alone, a dental anthropologist can gather all sorts of information. They can decipher migration patterns and cultural norms. They can tell if you ate with your fingers or if you endured famine. Our teeth are biographies.
